In this note, we extend our data model to include a vector of covariates and
then use them to construct a least-squares estimator for a linear combination of
treatment-group means. The resulting estimator has smaller conservative
asymptotic variance than either the unadjusted treatment-group-means estimator
or CUPED.

# Model

In addition to $(D_i,Y_i)$, suppose that for each unit we observe a $k$-dimensional vector of covariates $\mathbf{w}_i\in\mathbb{R}^k$. Unlike the outcome $Y_i$, the observed covariate vector $\mathbf{w}_i$ is assumed to be unaffected by treatment assignment. In practice, this condition is often satisfied by constructing $\mathbf{w}_i$ from information recorded before unit $i$ was first assigned a treatment group. We treat the sequence $\{\mathbf{w}_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ as fixed, so treatment assignment remains the only source of randomness in the model.

Let $\overline{\mathbf w}_n$ denote the covariate mean vector:
$$
\overline{\mathbf w}_n
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf w_i.
$$ {#eq-regression-covariate-mean}

Also define the centered covariate matrix and the
potential-outcome vectors

$$
\mathbf W_n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
(\mathbf w_1-\overline{\mathbf w}_n)' \\
\vdots \\
(\mathbf w_n-\overline{\mathbf w}_n)'
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf y_{0,n}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y_{1,0} \\
\vdots \\
y_{n,0}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf y_{1,n}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y_{1,1} \\
\vdots \\
y_{n,1}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Let

$$
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
=
\left(\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n
\right)^\dagger
\mathbf W_n'\mathbf y_{d,n}
$$
denote the vector of linear projection
coefficients, where $A^\dagger$ denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of a matrix $A$.
$\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}$ minimizes the sum of squared residuals:
$$
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
\in
\underset{\boldsymbol b\in\mathbb R^k}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
y_{i,d}
-\overline y_{d,n}
-\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol b
\right]^2.
$$ {#eq-regression-projection-minimization}

Define the corresponding residuals by
$$
\epsilon_{i,d,n}
=
y_{i,d}
-\overline y_{d,n}
-\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
$$ {#eq-regression-projection-residuals}

Summing over $i$, we obtain

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_{i,d,n}
=0.
$$ {#eq-regression-population-residual-sum-zero}

The first-order conditions for the minimization problem in
(-@eq-regression-projection-minimization) also imply
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)
\epsilon_{i,d,n}
=\mathbf0.
$$ {#eq-regression-population-normal-equations}

Collect the residuals into the vector

$$
\boldsymbol\epsilon_{i,n}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\epsilon_{i,0,n} \\
\epsilon_{i,1,n}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

and define the second-moment matrix

$$
\mathbf V_n
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\boldsymbol\epsilon_{i,n}\boldsymbol\epsilon_{i,n}'
=
\begin{pmatrix}
v_{0,n}^2 & v_{01,n} \\
v_{01,n} & v_{1,n}^2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-regression-residual-second-moments}

Also define unit $i$'s covariate leverage by
$$
h_{i,n}
=
\frac{1}{n}
+
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)^\dagger
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right),
$$

Collect the model primitives into the parameter vector

$$
\theta
=
\left(
p,
\{y_{i,0}\}_{i=1}^\infty,
\{y_{i,1}\}_{i=1}^\infty,
\{\mathbf w_i\}_{i=1}^\infty
\right)
$$


and let

$$
\Theta
\subseteq
[\underline p,1-\underline p]
\times\mathbb R^\mathbb N
\times\mathbb R^\mathbb N
\times(\mathbb R^k)^\mathbb N
$$

denote the set of parameter configurations under consideration.
We replace [Assumption 3](../treatment-group-means/#asm-nondegenerate) with the following regularity conditions:

::: {.assumption #asm-regression-covariates}
**Assumption 3'' (Regularity)**

[**(i)**]{.part-label} **(Non-degeneracy)** There exists an index $N$ such that
$v_{d,n}^2>0$ for every $n\geq N$, $\theta\in\Theta$, and $d\in\{0,1\}$.

[**(ii)**]{.part-label} **(Maximum variance share)** For each $d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
\frac{|\epsilon_{i,d,n}|}{\sqrt n\,v_{d,n}}
=0
$$

[**(iii)**]{.part-label} **(Maximum leverage)**

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
 h_{i,n}
=0.
$$
:::

Part (i) ensures that the residual variances are nonzero for all sufficiently large sample sizes and is analogous to the non-degeneracy condition in Assumption 3.
Part (ii) is the direct analogue of the maximum variance-share condition in Assumption 3(ii), with projection residuals replacing centered potential outcomes.
Part (iii) is the covariate analogue of the maximum variance-share condition; indeed, when $k=1$, the two conditions are exactly equivalent with the centered potential outcome replaced by the centered covariate.
In the [Appendix](#sec-regression-stationary-ergodic-conditions), we show that
these restrictions hold on a set of arbitrarily high probability when the
potential outcomes and covariates are generated jointly by a stationary
ergodic process with finite second moments and positive residual variances.

# Estimator

In this section, we derive a least squares estimator
for a linear combination of treatment group means.
Rearrange (-@eq-regression-projection-residuals) to obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{i,d}
&=
\overline y_{d,n}
+
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
+
\epsilon_{i,d,n},
\qquad d\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-potential-outcome-decomposition-centered}

Plugging in to the observation equation from [Assumption 2](../treatment-group-means/#asm-sutva) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i
&= (1 - D_i) y_{i,0} + D_i y_{i,1} \\[1ex]
&=
\left[
(1-D_i)\overline y_{0,n}
+D_i\overline y_{1,n}
\right]
\\
&\quad+
\left[
(1-D_i)
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}
+D_i
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}
\right]
\\
&\quad+
\left[
(1-D_i)\epsilon_{i,0,n}
+D_i\epsilon_{i,1,n}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-observed-outcome-projection-decomposition}

Because $\mathbf a_n\neq\mathbf0$, the vectors $(a_{0,n},a_{1,n})'$ and $(-a_{1,n},a_{0,n})'$ form an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb R^2$.
Define $\lambda_n$ via the change of coordinates

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi_n \\
\lambda_n
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0,n} & a_{1,n} \\
-a_{1,n} & a_{0,n}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline y_{0,n} \\
\overline y_{1,n}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-regression-mean-reparameterization}

Inverting this transformation yields

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline y_{0,n} \\
\overline y_{1,n}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\frac{1}{a_{0,n}^2+a_{1,n}^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
 a_{0,n} & -a_{1,n} \\
 a_{1,n} & a_{0,n}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi_n \\
\lambda_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-regression-mean-reparameterization-inverse}

We can therefore re-write the first term in (-@eq-regression-observed-outcome-projection-decomposition) as
$$
\begin{aligned}
(1-D_i)\overline y_{0,n}+D_i\overline y_{1,n}
&=
\psi_n D_i^{\psi} +
\lambda_n D_i^{\lambda}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-transformed-means}

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{i,n}^{\psi}
&=
\frac{a_{0,n}(1-D_i)+a_{1,n}D_i}
{a_{0,n}^2+a_{1,n}^2},
\\[2ex]
D_{i,n}^{\lambda}
&=
\frac{-a_{1,n}(1-D_i)+a_{0,n}D_i}
{a_{0,n}^2+a_{1,n}^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-transformed-treatment-regressors}

For the control mean, treatment mean, and ATE, respectively, these regressors
simplify to

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\psi_n
& D_{i,n}^{\psi}
& D_{i,n}^{\lambda}
\\ \hline
\overline y_{0,n}
& 1-D_i
& D_i
\\[1ex]
\overline y_{1,n}
& D_i
& -(1-D_i)
\\[1ex]
\overline y_{1,n}-\overline y_{0,n}
& D_i-\frac{1}{2}
& -\frac{1}{2}.
\end{array}
$$

Plugging into (-@eq-regression-observed-outcome-projection-decomposition) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i
&= \psi_nD_{i,n}^{\psi} + \lambda_nD_{i,n}^{\lambda} + (1-D_i)\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n} \\
&\quad\, + D_i\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n} + U_{i,n}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-fully-interacted-observed-outcome}
where
$$
U_{i,n}
=
(1-D_i)\epsilon_{i,0,n}
+D_i\epsilon_{i,1,n}.
$$

Now define the vectors

$$
\mathbf D_n^\psi
=
\begin{pmatrix}
D_{1,n}^{\psi} \\
\vdots \\
D_{n,n}^{\psi}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf D_n^\lambda
=
\begin{pmatrix}
D_{1,n}^{\lambda} \\
\vdots \\
D_{n,n}^{\lambda}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf D_n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
D_1 \\
\vdots \\
D_n
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf 1_n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\
\vdots \\
1
\end{pmatrix}
$$
and use them to construct the design matrix corresponding to (-@eq-regression-fully-interacted-observed-outcome):
$$
\mathbf X_n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf D_n^\psi
&
\mathbf D_n^\lambda
&
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n)\mathbf W_n
&
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf D_n)\mathbf W_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The regression estimator is defined as

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat\lambda_n \\
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,n} \\
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{1,n}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\left[
\left(\mathbf X_n\right)'
\mathbf X_n
\right]^\dagger
\left(\mathbf X_n\right)'
\mathbf Y_n,
$$ {#eq-regression-fully-interacted-estimator}
where
$$
\mathbf Y_n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
Y_1 \\
\vdots \\
Y_n
\end{pmatrix}
$$

In the [Appendix](#sec-regression-separate-regressions), we show that, with
probability approaching one uniformly over $\Theta$, $\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}$ can alternatively be computed by running
separate regressions for the control and treatment groups and then weighting the resulting
intercepts by $a_{0,n}$ and $a_{1,n}$, respectively.

## Treatment-group intercepts

It will be convenient to transform the estimated coefficients into the implied treatment-group intercepts using the inverse
transformation in (-@eq-regression-mean-reparameterization-inverse):

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\frac{1}{a_{0,n}^2+a_{1,n}^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0,n} & -a_{1,n} \\
a_{1,n} & a_{0,n}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat\lambda_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-regression-implied-intercepts}

In the [Appendix](#sec-regression-full-intercept-adjustment), we show

$$
\widehat\alpha_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\widehat y_{d,n}
-
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n},
$$ {#eq-regression-intercept-adjustments}
where

$$
\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}
=
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^nD_{i,d}\mathbf w_i
$$
denotes the covariate means in treatment group $d \in \{0, 1\}$.
The intercept estimator therefore adjusts the treatment-group mean $\widehat y_{d,n}$
by subtracting the covariate imbalance weighted by the treatment-group-specific
coefficient $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}$.

# Inference

## Error decomposition

In this section, we decompose the estimator's error into a weighted combination
of residual means and a remainder term.
Averaging (-@eq-regression-potential-outcome-decomposition-centered) over
treatment group $d$ gives

$$
\widehat y_{d,n}
=
\overline y_{d,n}
+
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
+
\widehat\epsilon_{d,n},
$$
where
$$
\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}
=
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^nD_{i,d}\epsilon_{i,d,n}.
$$


Substituting this expression into the first identity in
(-@eq-regression-intercept-adjustments) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\alpha_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
&=
\overline y_{d,n}
-
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right) +
\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-full-intercept-error}

Plugging into
$\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
=a_{0,n}\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+a_{1,n}\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$,
we obtain

$$
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}-\psi_n
=
[a_{0,n}\widehat\epsilon_{0,n}
+a_{1,n}\widehat\epsilon_{1,n}]
+R_n^{\mathrm{reg}},
$$ {#eq-regression-full-target-error-decomposition}

where

$$
R_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
-a_{0,n}
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{0,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}\right)
-a_{1,n}
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{1,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{1,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}\right).
$$ {#eq-regression-full-remainder-definition}

## Normality approximation

The leading term in
(-@eq-regression-full-target-error-decomposition) applies the treatment-group-means estimator to the residual arrays
$\{\epsilon_{i,0,n}\}$ and $\{\epsilon_{i,1,n}\}$. The row-wise means of these arrays are
zero by (-@eq-regression-population-residual-sum-zero), while
Assumption
3''(i) and (ii) provide the non-degeneracy and maximum variance-share
conditions needed to apply the results from the [treatment-group-means note](../treatment-group-means/#sec-estimator-asymptotics).
Define

$$
\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{1-p_d}{p_d}v_{d,n}^2,
\qquad
\sigma_{01,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=v_{01,n}.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-treatment-group-variance}

The variance of the leading term in
(-@eq-regression-full-target-error-decomposition) is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
&=
a_{0,n}^2\sigma_{0,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
+a_{1,n}^2\sigma_{1,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
-2a_{0,n}a_{1,n}\sigma_{01,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-full-treatment-group-means-variance}

The corresponding conservative variance is

$$
\widetilde\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\left(
|a_{0,n}|\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+|a_{1,n}|\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-conservative-variance}

If the projection residuals were observed, we could estimate the
treatment-group-specific variances by

$$
\check\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{1-\overline D_{d,n}}{\overline D_{d,n}}
\left[
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}\left(\epsilon_{i,d,n}-\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}\right)^2
\right],
\qquad d\in\{0,1\},
$$ {#eq-regression-full-oracle-treatment-group-variance-estimator}

and construct

$$
\check\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\left(
|a_{0,n}|\check\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+|a_{1,n}|\check\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-oracle-conservative-variance-estimator}

The
[studentized normal approximation](../treatment-group-means/#eq-feasible-normal-approximation){.quarto-xref} from the treatment-group-means note implies

$$
\sqrt n
\frac{
a_{0,n}\widehat\epsilon_{0,n}
+a_{1,n}\widehat\epsilon_{1,n}
}{\check\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
Z_n^{\mathrm{reg}},
\qquad
Z_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
\sim
N\left(
0,
\frac{\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widetilde\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
\right).
$$ {#eq-regression-full-oracle-normal-approximation}

$\check\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}$ is infeasible
because the projection residuals are unobserved. To obtain a feasible
estimator, we replace the population residuals with the fitted residuals:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat U_{i,n}
&=
Y_i
-\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}D_{i,n}^{\psi}
-\widehat\lambda_nD_{i,n}^{\lambda}
\\
&\quad-
(1-D_i)
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,n}
-D_i
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{1,n}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-full-fitted-residual}

Define the feasible within-treatment-group fitted-residual variances by

$$
\widehat v_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}\left(\widehat U_{i,n}\right)^2
$$ {#eq-regression-full-sample-residual-variances}

and construct

$$
\widehat\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{1-\overline D_{d,n}}{\overline D_{d,n}}
\widehat v_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}},
\qquad
\widehat\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\left(
|a_{0,n}|\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+|a_{1,n}|\widehat\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-conservative-variance-estimator}

In the [Appendix](#sec-regression-oracle-feasible-arm-variance), we show that

$$
\frac{\check\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-oracle-feasible-variance-consistency}

Since $\check\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}$ and
$\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}$ are nonnegative,
@prp-continuous-mapping(i) gives
$\check\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}/\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1$. Moreover,
$\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}\leq\widetilde\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}$
implies $Z_n^{\mathrm{reg}}=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$. Therefore
(-@eq-regression-full-oracle-normal-approximation) and
@prp-asymptotic-equivalence-slutsky imply

$$
\sqrt n
\frac{
a_{0,n}\widehat\epsilon_{0,n}
+a_{1,n}\widehat\epsilon_{1,n}
}{\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
Z_n^{\mathrm{reg}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-feasible-residual-means-normal-approximation}

## Confidence intervals

The [Appendix](#sec-regression-remainder-negligibility) shows that the remainder term is negligible:

$$
\frac{\sqrt n\,R_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}0.
$$ {#eq-regression-remainder-negligibility}

Combining
(-@eq-regression-full-target-error-decomposition), (-@eq-regression-full-feasible-residual-means-normal-approximation) and (-@eq-regression-remainder-negligibility) and applying
@prp-asymptotic-equivalence-perturbation gives

$$
\sqrt n
\frac{\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}-\psi_n}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
Z_n^{\mathrm{reg}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-feasible-normal-approximation}

Define the confidence interval by

$$
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\left[
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
-z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}{n}},
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
+z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}{n}}
\right].
$$ {#eq-regression-confidence-interval}

The uniform-coverage argument from the treatment-group-means note then gives

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_\theta\left(\psi_n\in C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)
\geq 1-\alpha.
$$ {#eq-regression-confidence-interval-coverage}

# Comparison with other estimators

In this section, we compare the regression estimator with two alternatives: the
unadjusted treatment-group-means estimator and CUPED.

## Unadjusted estimator

We first compare the conservative variance of the regression estimator with
that of the unadjusted treatment-group-means estimator.
Squaring the decomposition in
(-@eq-regression-potential-outcome-decomposition-centered) and applying the
population normal equations in (-@eq-regression-population-normal-equations)
gives, for each $d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_{i,d}-\overline y_{d,n}\right)^2
=
v_{d,n}^2
+\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}'
\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}.
$$ {#eq-regression-adjusted-residual-second-moments}

Define the finite-population coefficient of determination for treatment group
$d$ as

$$
R_{d,n}^2
=
\frac{
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}'
\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
}{
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_{i,d}-\overline y_{d,n}\right)^2
}
.
$$

The two terms on the right-hand side of
(-@eq-regression-adjusted-residual-second-moments) are nonnegative, so
$0\leq R_{d,n}^2\leq 1$. Rearranging gives

$$
v_{d,n}^2
=
(1-R_{d,n}^2)
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_{i,d}-\overline y_{d,n}\right)^2.
$$

Using (-@eq-regression-full-treatment-group-variance), we then have

$$
\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\left(1-R_{d,n}^2\right)\sigma_{d,n}^2.
$$

The conservative regression variance in
(-@eq-regression-full-conservative-variance) therefore satisfies

$$
\widetilde\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\left(
|a_{0,n}|\sqrt{1-R_{0,n}^2}\,\sigma_{0,n}
+|a_{1,n}|\sqrt{1-R_{1,n}^2}\,\sigma_{1,n}
\right)^2.
$$

Taking nonnegative square roots and rearranging, we obtain

$$
\frac{\widetilde\sigma_n - \widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}{\widetilde\sigma_n}
=
w_{0,n}\left(1-\sqrt{1-R_{0,n}^2}\right)
+w_{1,n}\left(1-\sqrt{1-R_{1,n}^2}\right),
$$
where

$$
w_{d,n}
=
\frac{|a_{d,n}|\sigma_{d,n}}{|a_{d,n}|\sigma_{d,n}+|a_{1-d,n}|\sigma_{1-d,n}}
,
\qquad d\in\{0,1\},
$$

denotes the share of the unadjusted conservative standard deviation contributed by
treatment group $d$.
The relative reduction in the conservative standard deviation is therefore a
weighted average of the armwise reduction factors $1-\sqrt{1-R_{d,n}^2}$.
Taking a first-order expansion around $R_{d,n}^2=0$ yields

$$
1-\sqrt{1-R_{d,n}^2}
=
\frac{R_{d,n}^2}{2}
+O\left(R_{d,n}^4\right).
$$

Thus, when both armwise $R^2$ values are small, the relative reduction in the
conservative standard deviation is approximately

$$
\frac{\widetilde\sigma_n - \widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}{\widetilde\sigma_n}
\approx
\frac{w_{0,n}R_{0,n}^2+w_{1,n}R_{1,n}^2}{2}.
$$

## CUPED

[CUPED](https://doi.org/10.1145/2433396.2433413) is a commonly used technique that reduces variance by
subtracting a covariate adjustment from each treatment-group mean.
Let

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_n
=
\left(\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)^\dagger
\mathbf W_n'\mathbf Y_n.
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-coefficient-estimator}

denote the pooled coefficient estimator and
define the CUPED-adjusted treatment-group mean by

$$
\widehat\alpha_{d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
=
\widehat y_{d,n}
-\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_n,
\qquad d\in\{0,1\}.
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-intercept}

Compared with the regression intercepts in
(-@eq-regression-intercept-adjustments), the CUPED intercepts replace the
treatment-group-specific coefficient $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}$ with a single coefficient vector shared across treatment groups.
The CUPED estimator of $\psi_n$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{cuped}}
&=
a_{0,n}\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
+a_{1,n}\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-estimator}

To describe its asymptotic behavior, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\gamma_n
&=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_n\right]
\\
&=
\left(\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)^\dagger
\mathbf W_n'
\left[(1-p)\mathbf y_{0,n}+p\mathbf y_{1,n}\right]
\\
&=
(1-p)\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}
+p\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-standard-cuped-coefficient}

Averaging (-@eq-regression-potential-outcome-decomposition-centered) over
treatment group $d$ and substituting the result into
(-@eq-regression-cuped-intercept) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\alpha_{d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
&=
\overline y_{d,n}
+\widehat u_{d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
-\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_n-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-residual}

where
$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat u_{d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
&=
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}},
\\[1ex]
u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
&=
\epsilon_{i,d,n}
+\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)
\end{aligned}
$$


Consequently,

$$
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{cuped}}-\psi_n
=
a_{0,n}\widehat u_{0,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
+a_{1,n}\widehat u_{1,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
+R_n^{\mathrm{cuped}},
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-error-decomposition}

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_n^{\mathrm{cuped}}
&=
-a_{0,n}
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{0,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_n-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)
\\
&\quad-
a_{1,n}
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{1,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_n-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-remainder}

Define

$$
\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{cuped}}
=
\frac{1-p_d}{p_d}
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}\right)^2
\right)
$$

Because $\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}$ is the projection coefficient, the population
normal equations (-@eq-regression-population-normal-equations) make
$\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n$ orthogonal to $\epsilon_{i,d,n}$.
Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}\right)^2
&=
v_{d,n}^2
+
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)'
\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-second-moments}

which implies
$$
\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{cuped}}
=
\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}
+
\frac{1-p_d}{p_d}
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)'
\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right).
$$

The quadratic form is nonnegative, so
$\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{cuped}}\geq\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}$ for each
$d\in\{0,1\}$. Consequently, the conservative CUPED variance satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{cuped}}
&=
\left(
|a_{0,n}|\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
+|a_{1,n}|\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{cuped}}
\right)^2
\\
&\geq
\left(
|a_{0,n}|\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+|a_{1,n}|\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)^2
\\
&=
\widetilde\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-cuped-conservative-variance}

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf W_n\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)
&=
p\,\mathbf W_n
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}\right),
\\[1ex]
\mathbf W_n\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}-\boldsymbol\gamma_n\right)
&=
-(1-p)\,\mathbf W_n
\left(\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

$\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{cuped}} = \sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}$ if and only if

$$
\mathbf W_n\boldsymbol\beta_{0,n}
=
\mathbf W_n\boldsymbol\beta_{1,n}.
$$

The regression estimator therefore has weakly smaller conservative asymptotic
variance than the CUPED estimator, with strict inequality whenever the linear projections differ across treatment groups.

# Appendix

## A mixture-model motivation for [Assumption 3''](#asm-regression-covariates) {#sec-regression-stationary-ergodic-conditions}

Let $\mathcal Q$ be a collection of probability laws on the path space
$(\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^k)^\mathbb N$. Under each $Q\in\mathcal Q$,
suppose the joint coordinate process

$$
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
Y_{i,0} \\
Y_{i,1} \\
W_i
\end{pmatrix}
:i\geq1
\right\}
$$

is stationary and ergodic. Suppose also that, for each $d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\mathbb E_Q\left[Y_{1,d}^2\right]<\infty,
\qquad
\mathbb E_Q\left[\|W_1\|^2\right]<\infty.
$$

Define

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mu_d(Q)
=
\mathbb E_Q[Y_{1,d}],
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)
=
\mathbb E_Q[W_1],
\\[2ex]
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)
=
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)'
\right],
\\[2ex]
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)
=
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)^\dagger
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)
\right],
\\[2ex]
v_d^2(Q)
=
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left\{
Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)
-\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)
\right\}^2
\right],
\end{gathered}
$$

and assume $v_d^2(Q)>0$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability distribution on
$\mathcal Q$. Generate a path of potential outcomes and covariates by first
drawing $Q\sim\Pi$ and then drawing the path according to $Q$.

For each $d\in\{0,1\}$, define the empirical quantities

$$
\begin{gathered}
\overline Y_{d,n}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nY_{i,d},
\qquad
\overline W_n
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nW_i,
\\[2ex]
\mathbf Y_{d,n}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
Y_{1,d} \\
\vdots \\
Y_{n,d}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbb W_n
=
\begin{pmatrix}
(W_1-\overline W_n)' \\
\vdots \\
(W_n-\overline W_n)'
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{gathered}
$$

We use the existing notation $\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}$,
$\epsilon_{i,d,n}$, $v_{d,n}^2$, and $h_{i,n}$ for the corresponding
functions of these random empirical data.

### Projection coefficient convergence

We first show that

$$
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\to\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)
$$ {#eq-regression-ergodic-coefficient-convergence}
$Q$-almost surely.
The ergodic theorem gives

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n
\to
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)
\\[2ex]
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbf Y_{d,n}
\to
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)
\right]
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-regression-ergodic-projection-moment-convergence}
$Q$-almost surely.
Let

$$
r
=
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)).
$$

We consider three cases.

**Case 1: full rank**. If $r=k$, $\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)$ is positive definite. The empirical
covariance matrix is therefore positive definite for all sufficiently large
$n$, and continuity of matrix inversion gives

$$
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n
\right)^{-1}
\to
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)^{-1}.
$$

For all such $n$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
&=
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n
\right)^{-1}
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbf Y_{d,n}
\right)
\\[1ex]
&\to
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)^{-1}
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)
\right]
\\[1ex]
&=
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q).
\end{aligned}
$$

**Case 2: zero rank**. If $r=0$, then $\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)=\mathbf0$, so
$W_i=\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)$ simultaneously for every $i\geq1$,
$Q$-almost surely. Hence $\mathbb W_n=\mathbf0$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}=\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)=\mathbf0$ for every $n$.

**Case 3: intermediate rank**. Suppose instead that $0<r<k$.
Since the Moore--Penrose inverse is continuous along fixed-rank sequences, it
suffices to show that the empirical covariance matrix
$\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n$ has rank $r$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, $Q$-almost surely.
Toward this end, let
$\left\{\mathbf q_1(Q),\ldots,\mathbf q_{k-r}(Q)\right\}$ be an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{null}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q))$. For each
$j\in\{1,\ldots,k-r\}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
0
&=
\mathbf q_j(Q)'\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)\mathbf q_j(Q)
\\
&=
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left\{
\mathbf q_j(Q)'
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\right\}^2
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for all $j\in\{1,\ldots,k-r\}$,

$$
\mathbf q_j(Q)'
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
=0
$$

$Q$-almost surely. Hence

$$
W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)
\in
\operatorname{null}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q))^\perp
=
\operatorname{col}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q))
$$

$Q$-almost surely. By stationarity and countable subadditivity, this inclusion holds simultaneously for every $i\geq1$, $Q$-almost surely. On this probability-one event,

$$
\overline W_n-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(W_i-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\in
\operatorname{col}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q))
$$

and

$$
W_i-\overline W_n
=
\left(W_i-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
-
\left(\overline W_n-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\in
\operatorname{col}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)).
$$

Consequently,

$$
0
\leq
\operatorname{rank}\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n\right)
=
\operatorname{rank}(\mathbb W_n)
\leq
r.
$$ {#eq-regression-ergodic-covariance-rank-upper-bound}

Let $\lambda_r(A)$ denote the $r$th largest eigenvalue of a
symmetric matrix $A$. Since $\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)$ has rank $r>0$,

$$
\lambda_r\left(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)\right)>0.
$$

Convergence of the empirical covariance matrix implies

$$
\lambda_r\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n\right)
\to
\lambda_r\left(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)\right)>0.
$$

Therefore, for all sufficiently large $n$,

$$
\operatorname{rank}\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n\right)
\geq r.
$$

Combining this inequality with
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-covariance-rank-upper-bound) gives

$$
\operatorname{rank}\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n\right)
=
r
=
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q))
$$

for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence
$$
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n
\right)^\dagger
\to
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)^\dagger,
$$
which implies
$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}
&=
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n
\right)^\dagger
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbf Y_{d,n}
\right)
\\[1ex]
&\to
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)^\dagger
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)
\right]
\\[1ex]
&=
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q).
\end{aligned}
$$

### Residual-variance convergence

We next show that the residual variance converges to the population value $Q$-almost surely. Expanding the square gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{d,n}^2
&=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(Y_{i,d}-\overline Y_{d,n}\right)^2 -
2\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}'
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbf Y_{d,n}
\right) +
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}'
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n
\right)
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The ergodic theorem also gives

$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(Y_{i,d}-\overline Y_{d,n}\right)^2
\to
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)^2
\right]
$$

$Q$-almost surely. Combining this limit with
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-coefficient-convergence) and
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-projection-moment-convergence) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{d,n}^2
&\to
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)^2
\right]
\\[1ex]
&\quad-
2\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)'
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)
\left(Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)\right)
\right]
\\[1ex]
&\quad+
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)'
\boldsymbol\Sigma_w(Q)
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)
\\[1ex]
&=
\mathbb E_Q\left[
\left\{
Y_{1,d}-\mu_d(Q)
-
\left(W_1-\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_d(Q)
\right\}^2
\right]
\\
&=
v_d^2(Q).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ergodic-residual-variance-convergence}

$Q$-almost surely for each $d\in\{0,1\}$.

### Maximum variance-share and leverage conditions

We next show the maximum variance-share and maximum-leverage conditions
hold $Q$-almost surely.
The dyadic union-bound and Borel--Cantelli argument used in the
[mixture-model motivation for Assumption 3](../treatment-group-means/#sec-stationary-ergodic-conditions)
applies to every coordinate of the joint process. The finite-second-moment
conditions therefore imply

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
\left(
|Y_{i,0}|+|Y_{i,1}|+\|W_i\|
\right)
\to 0
$$

$Q$-almost surely. The ergodic theorem also gives

$$
\overline Y_{d,n}
\to
\mu_d(Q),
\qquad
\overline W_n
\to
\boldsymbol\mu_w(Q)
$$

$Q$-almost surely. On every path for which these convergences hold, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
|\epsilon_{i,d,n}|
&\leq
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|Y_{i,d}|
+
\frac{|\overline Y_{d,n}|}{\sqrt n}
\\
&\quad+
\|\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\|
\left(
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|W_i\|
+
\frac{\|\overline W_n\|}{\sqrt n}
\right)
\\
&\to 0.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ergodic-residual-maximum}

Together with the positive limit in
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-residual-variance-convergence), this gives

$$
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
\frac{|\epsilon_{i,d,n}|}{\sqrt n\,v_{d,n}}
\to 0
$$

$Q$-almost surely.

For leverage, suppose first that $r>0$. The convergence results above imply that
$\left\|\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n\right)^\dagger\right\|$
is bounded for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}h_{i,n}
&\leq
\frac{1}{n}
+
\left\|
\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbb W_n'\mathbb W_n\right)^\dagger
\right\|
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
\frac{\|W_i-\overline W_n\|^2}{n}
\to 0.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ergodic-leverage}
$Q$-almost surely.

When $r=0$, $h_{i,n}=1/n$, so the same conclusion holds.

### Uniformity over $\Theta$

Let $\mathbb P_{\mathbf Y,\mathbf W}$ denote the mixture law of the path. The
events on which the convergences in
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-residual-variance-convergence),
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-residual-maximum), and
(-@eq-regression-ergodic-leverage) hold are measurable and have $Q$-probability
one for every $Q\in\mathcal Q$. Their intersection, taken over $d\in\{0,1\}$
where applicable, therefore has probability one under
$\mathbb P_{\mathbf Y,\mathbf W}$.

For a realized path $(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)$, define the measurable pathwise
limit

$$
V_d^*(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)
=
\limsup_{n\to\infty}v_{d,n}^2.
$$

Then $0<V_d^*(\mathbf Y,\mathbf W)<\infty$ almost surely. The same
continuity-from-below and Egorov argument used in the
[mixture-model motivation for Assumption 3](../treatment-group-means/#sec-stationary-ergodic-conditions)
shows that, for every $\eta>0$, there exist $c>0$ and a measurable set $E$
such that $\mathbb P_{\mathbf Y,\mathbf W}(E)>1-\eta$ and, for
$d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\inf_{(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)\in E}V_d^*(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)\geq c,
\\
\sup_{(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)\in E}
\left|v_{d,n}^2-V_d^*(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)\right|
\to0,
\\
\sup_{(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)\in E}
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|\epsilon_{i,d,n}|
\to0,
\qquad
\sup_{(\mathbf y,\mathbf w)\in E}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}h_{i,n}
\to0.
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-regression-uniform-pathwise-convergences}

Let $\Theta$ be the set of parameter configurations whose treatment probability
satisfies Assumption 1 and whose potential-outcome and covariate path lies in
$E$.
(-@eq-regression-uniform-pathwise-convergences) implies that this $\Theta$
satisfies Assumption 3''.
Thus, for every $\eta>0$, the mixture law assigns probability greater than
$1-\eta$ to a set of paths that induces a parameter space satisfying
Assumption 3''.

## Separate-regression representation {#sec-regression-separate-regressions}

We first show that the intercept and effective covariate coefficients are
uniquely identified within each treatment group with probability approaching
one uniformly over $\Theta$. Let

$$
r_n
=
\operatorname{rank}\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n\right)
$$

and fix a reduced eigendecomposition

$$
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf W_n'\mathbf W_n
=
\mathbf U_n\boldsymbol\Lambda_n\mathbf U_n',
$$

where the columns of $\mathbf U_n\in\mathbb R^{k\times r_n}$ are orthonormal
and $\boldsymbol\Lambda_n\in\mathbb R^{r_n\times r_n}$ is diagonal and
positive definite. If $r_n=0$, then $\mathbf W_n=\mathbf0$. In that case,
the two treatment-group intercepts are uniquely identified whenever both
treatment groups are nonempty, an event whose probability approaches one
uniformly. Suppose below that $r_n>0$, and define

$$
\mathbf z_{i,n}
=
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{-1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right),
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}
=
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^nD_{i,d}\mathbf z_{i,n}.
$$

Then

$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf z_{i,n}=\mathbf0,
\qquad
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\mathbf z_{i,n}\mathbf z_{i,n}'
=\mathbf I_{r_n},
\qquad
h_{i,n}
=
\frac{1+\|\mathbf z_{i,n}\|^2}{n}.
$$

For each $d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\mathbb E_\theta
\left\|
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(D_{i,d}-p_d)\mathbf z_{i,n}
\right\|^2
=
\frac{p_d(1-p_d)r_n}{n}
\leq
\frac{k}{4n},
$$

so $n^{-1}\sum_iD_{i,d}\mathbf z_{i,n}=o_{\mathcal P}(1)$.
Because $\overline D_{d,n}\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}p_d$ and
$p_d\geq\underline p$, @prp-joint-convergence(i) and
@prp-continuous-mapping(i) give
$\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}=o_{\mathcal P}(1)$. Moreover,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_\theta
\left\|
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(D_{i,d}-p_d)\mathbf z_{i,n}\mathbf z_{i,n}'
\right\|_{\mathrm F}^2
\\
&\qquad=
\frac{p_d(1-p_d)}{n^2}
\sum_{i=1}^n\|\mathbf z_{i,n}\|^4
\\
&\qquad\leq
\frac{k}{4}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
\frac{\|\mathbf z_{i,n}\|^2}{n}
\leq
\frac{k}{4}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}h_{i,n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Assumption 3''(iii) therefore implies

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}
\left(\mathbf z_{i,n}-\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right)
\left(\mathbf z_{i,n}-\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right)'
\\
&\qquad=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}\mathbf z_{i,n}\mathbf z_{i,n}'
-
\overline D_{d,n}
\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}'
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}
p_d\mathbf I_{r_n}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-arm-effective-covariate-rank}

uniformly over $\Theta$. Since $p_d\geq\underline p$, both armwise centered
matrices in (-@eq-regression-arm-effective-covariate-rank) are positive
definite with probability approaching one uniformly. On this event, no
nonzero effective linear combination of the covariates is constant within a
treatment group. Hence the intercept and effective slope are uniquely
identified in each of the two separate treatment-group regressions. Any
remaining slope nonuniqueness belongs to $\operatorname{null}(\mathbf W_n)$
and does not affect the fitted values or intercepts.

After permuting observations by treatment group, the fully interacted
least-squares criterion is the sum of the two separate treatment-group
criteria. The unique intercepts and effective slopes must therefore agree
with those from the two separate regressions. Finally,
(-@eq-regression-implied-intercepts) gives

$$
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
a_{0,n}\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+
a_{1,n}\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}},
$$

which proves the claimed representation.

## Fully interacted intercept adjustment {#sec-regression-full-intercept-adjustment}

By the definitions of $D_{i,n}^{\psi}$ and
$D_{i,n}^{\lambda}$,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf D_n^\psi & \mathbf D_n^\lambda
\end{pmatrix}
'
=
\frac{1}{a_{0,n}^2+a_{1,n}^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0,n} & -a_{1,n} \\
a_{1,n} & a_{0,n}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n & \mathbf D_n
\end{pmatrix}
'
$$ {#eq-regression-treatment-column-transformation}

Together with (-@eq-regression-implied-intercepts), this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf D_n^\psi\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\mathbf D_n^\lambda\widehat\lambda_n
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n & \mathbf D_n
\end{pmatrix}
\frac{1}{a_{0,n}^2+a_{1,n}^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{0,n} & -a_{1,n} \\
a_{1,n} & a_{0,n}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat\lambda_n
\end{pmatrix}
\\[1ex]
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n & \mathbf D_n
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\end{pmatrix}
\\[1ex]
&=
(\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n)\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\mathbf D_n\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-full-fitted-treatment-group-intercepts}

The fully interacted estimator solves the least-squares problem

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat\lambda_n \\
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,n} \\
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{1,n}
\end{pmatrix}
\in
\underset{\boldsymbol b\in\mathbb R^{2+2k}}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\left\|
\mathbf Y_n-\mathbf X_n\boldsymbol b
\right\|^2
$$ {#eq-regression-full-least-squares-problem}

The first-order conditions for
(-@eq-regression-full-least-squares-problem) imply

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf D_n^\psi & \mathbf D_n^\lambda
\end{pmatrix}
'
\left[
\mathbf Y_n
-\mathbf D_n^\psi\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
-\mathbf D_n^\lambda\widehat\lambda_n
-\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n)
\mathbf W_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,n}
-\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf D_n)
\mathbf W_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{1,n}
\right]
= \mathbf{0}.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-transformed-treatment-normal-equations}

Equations (-@eq-regression-treatment-column-transformation),
(-@eq-regression-full-fitted-treatment-group-intercepts), and
(-@eq-regression-full-transformed-treatment-normal-equations) imply

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n & \mathbf D_n
\end{pmatrix}
'
\left[
\mathbf Y_n
-(\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n)\widehat\alpha_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-\mathbf D_n\widehat\alpha_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf 1_n-\mathbf D_n)
\mathbf W_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,n}
-\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf D_n)
\mathbf W_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{1,n}
\right]
= \mathbf{0}.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-treatment-arm-normal-equations}

Dividing the two normal equations by the corresponding treatment-group sample
sizes gives, for each $d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\frac{1}{n_d}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}
\left[
Y_i
-\widehat\alpha_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-\left(\mathbf w_i-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}
\right]
=0.
$$ {#eq-regression-full-treatment-arm-normal-equations-intercepts}

Evaluating the sum and rearranging yields
(-@eq-regression-intercept-adjustments).

## Equivalence of oracle and fitted-residual variances {#sec-regression-oracle-feasible-arm-variance}

We show that replacing the centered projection residuals by the fully
interacted fitted residuals has no asymptotic effect. The
[separate-regression representation](#sec-regression-separate-regressions)
defines $r_n$, $\mathbf U_n$, $\boldsymbol\Lambda_n$, $\mathbf z_{i,n}$,
and $\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}$. If $r_n=0$, then $\mathbf W_n=\mathbf0$
and the fitted residuals equal
$\epsilon_{i,d,n}-\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}$ within
treatment group $d$.
Suppose below that $r_n>0$.

The treatment-group slope normal equations imply

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}
\left(\mathbf z_{i,n}-\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right)
\left(\mathbf z_{i,n}-\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right)'
\right]
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right)
\\
&\qquad=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}
\left(\mathbf z_{i,n}-\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right)
\left(\epsilon_{i,d,n}-\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The population normal equations give
$\sum_i\mathbf z_{i,n}\epsilon_{i,d,n}=\mathbf0$, so the
right-hand side
equals

$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(D_{i,d}-p_d)\mathbf z_{i,n}\epsilon_{i,d,n}
-
\overline D_{d,n}\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}
\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}.
$$

The first term has mean zero and satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_\theta
\left\|
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(D_{i,d}-p_d)\mathbf z_{i,n}\epsilon_{i,d,n}
\right\|^2
\\
&\qquad\leq
p_d(1-p_d)
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}h_{i,n}\,v_{d,n}^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Moreover,

$$
\sqrt n\,\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}=O_{\mathcal P}(1),
\qquad
\sqrt n\,\frac{|\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}|}{v_{d,n}}
=O_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$

Combining these bounds with Assumption 3''(iii) and
(-@eq-regression-arm-effective-covariate-rank) gives

$$
\frac{
\left\|
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right)
\right\|
}{v_{d,n}}
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$

For every unit assigned to treatment group $d$,
(-@eq-regression-full-fitted-residual) and
(-@eq-regression-full-intercept-error) give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat U_{i,n}
&=
\epsilon_{i,d,n}-\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}
\\
&\quad-
\left(\mathbf z_{i,n}-\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right)'
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The effective-slope bound, the treatment-group-means variance-consistency
result, and (-@eq-regression-arm-effective-covariate-rank) therefore imply

$$
\frac{\widehat v_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}{v_{d,n}^2}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1,
\qquad
\frac{
n_d^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}
\left(\epsilon_{i,d,n}-\widehat\epsilon_{d,n}\right)^2
}{v_{d,n}^2}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1.
$$

The treatment-share factor is the same in
$\check\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}$ and
$\widehat\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}$. Hence

$$
\frac{\check\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_{d,n}^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1,
\qquad d\in\{0,1\}.
$$

Taking nonnegative square roots and applying the weighted-sum definitions of
$\check\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}$ and
$\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}$ gives

$$
\frac{\check\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{2,\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1.
$$

## Regression remainders {#sec-regression-remainder-negligibility}

The effective-slope bounds established above, together with Assumption 1 and
the scale definitions, give, for each $d\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt n\,\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}
&=O_{\mathcal P}(1),
\\[2ex]
\frac{
\left\|
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right)
\right\|
}{\sigma_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
&=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

If $r_n=0$, then $\mathbf W_n=\mathbf0$ and the remainder is zero. If
$r_n>0$, the effective-coordinate definitions imply

$$
\left(\widehat{\mathbf w}_{d,n}-\overline{\mathbf w}_n\right)'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right)
=
\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}'
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right).
$$

The remainder definition therefore yields

$$
\frac{\sqrt n\,|R_n^{\mathrm{reg}}|}
{\widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\leq
\sum_{d\in\{0,1\}}
\frac{|a_{d,n}|\sigma_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\left\|\sqrt n\,\widehat{\mathbf z}_{d,n}\right\|
\frac{
\left\|
\boldsymbol\Lambda_n^{1/2}\mathbf U_n'
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{d,n}-\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}\right)
\right\|
}{\sigma_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$

In the sum, the two nonnegative coefficients add to one. The
[treatment-group-means variance-consistency result](../treatment-group-means/#eq-variance-ratio-consistency){.quarto-xref},
applied to the corresponding residual arrays, and the fitted-residual variance
equivalence proved above imply

$$
\frac{\widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1.
$$

It follows that

$$
\frac{\sqrt n\,R_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
=
\frac{\sqrt n\,R_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\frac{\widetilde\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_n^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}0.
$$
